messages.author: 321fe6c60966e560
messages.subject: Re: range finders
parts:
Dear List,

Thanks so much for responding to my question, it was very helpful! I have
included all of the responses below. I welcome any additional comments.

Happy field days,
Kimberly Ferree

> > Can anyone recommend some decent range finders ($100-200)? We are working=

> > in forested habitat and typically record >10 individuals at each point
> > count station.

1) I have done a bit of bird monitoring down here in Tasmania in woodlands
and forests and used DISTANCE. Heaping of data is a common problem and
range finders reduce this so I figured a cheap solution. Here is a
snippet from my last report:

"For density calculations the program DISTANCE requires radial
distances to detections to be estimated accurately and previous results
often showed heaping of data at distances of 5, 10, 15, 20m. In order to
reduce this unwanted effect I calibrated the focus control of my
binoculars with distance-to-object by marking lines on the focus control
aligned with a fixed line on the body of the binoculars for various
focal distances. I was then able to more accurately estimate distances,
at least up to 20m. Even for audible detections this technique can
improve distance estimation since for most birds you can tell where the
sound is coming from even if you cannot see the bird."

Cost is $0!! unless of course you need to buy binoculars. So if you are
in forest habitat too I would suggest that 20 metres or whatever units
you use over there would be sufficient. You can of course only really
calibrate a particular pair of binoculars for your own eyes.

2) I recommend Bushnell=AE Laser Rangefinder Yardage Pro=AE 500's or 400's.
I've used both of these in grasslands, deserts and forests alike and they
are fantastic. I believe they cost a bit more than a few hundred dollars
(i.e., $300-$400), but they are well worth the money!

3) I have used the Bushnell Yardage Pro 800 for point counts and found it
to be easy to use and work very well. It also tested quite accurate
according to GPS readings I did. It has some nice features that allow
it to work in various conditions functioning in different modes, such
as through light rain, and it measures in meters. It lists for $349
through Forestry Suppliers so a bit more than your price range, but
worth the value.

Having said all that however, it should be noted that one must have an
un-obstructed visible target, which can be problematic in dense
forest. One can compensate in many instances by shooting a more
visible target at the same distance, such as an adjacent tree. Be
aware though, that lazer rangefinders may be of more value for
training than in practical use in dense vegetation and should not be a
substitute for pre-season training.

4) I got mine from binoculars.com - towards the upper end of your price
range, but cheaper than Amazon. It's excellent for up to around 300m.
In forest, you have to be careful, because you may get a reading to a
single leaf or twig that is some distance in front of the point you're
trying to measure to. See
http://binoculars.com/categories/Rangefinders.html
(Note: Steve Buckland sent this one)

5) I use lazer range finders regularly for small-medium sized mammals
during day and night work. The only range that I have found useful for
all situations and which has excellent optics is the Leica LRF series -
the current model being the Leica LRF 900. In the UK these cost =A3280 -
not cheap, but you'd not regret buying it and it'd last a lifetime. I've
compared these with 2 products from Bushnell and they just don't compare!

6) Bushnel Yardage Pro Scout; minimum distance is 10 m, maximum distance

is about 550 m. It has a scan mode and >150 mode that can be helpful
for far targets in moderate brush cover. I thing the unit is about
$140.

Sounds like you've have a good experience with the Scouts? We bought 4
the first year they came out (a mistake, granted) and were badly
disappointed -2 broke immediately, one was so inaccurate right out of
the box we sent it back for alignment and never saw it again. The 4th
worked well enough, but the batteries were soon expended and had to come
by in rural Utah counties. I'd be glad to hear they now work -the size
is still very attractive to the average gear-laden field tech...

-Russ

Well, the older models had a poor design with the on/off switch on the
cap to the batteries. That part broke on the older model I have but it
was very easy to fix. I also have a newer model that doesn't have that
problem because there is no on/off switch (it is on when in use and off
otherwise). As for battery problems, I have only had to replace the
batteries about once a year. I also have a Nikon 600 which is about
$250. It is good for closer distances (<100 m) because it records
distance in 0.5 m increments up to 99.5 m. However, it is difficult to
measure distances beyond 150-200 m with it.

Matt

7) Try at Bushnell's Yardage Pro series. They are inexpensive and work well
within about 200m range.

messages.subject: range finders
parts:
On this same subject, I have had trouble getting distances on small,
floating birds (<Laughing Gull size, like eared grebes) from a boat. Does
anyone have a suggestion for a range finder that works well on small objects
AND gets the distance quickly, as the movement of the boat can make this
difficult and there are not typically other objects that can be sited on.
